data.question: Should we adopt the rule change block_k 3 → 2 even though companies B and C voted against it, raise the constitutional floor min_company_on_time_rate from 0.6 to 0.65, or keep the current rules (v1)?
data.background: Proposal 2 passes check, the constitution and the KPI conditions, and raises the main goal on_time_deliveries by +9.2 on 5/5 seeds, but B and C voted it down. Whether to override two companies is an agreement between human parties, not something a measurement can settle. R1 changes a value in the constitution, and regulation changes must always be decided by a human; the current rules already meet the proposed floor.

options.summary: Lower the blocking_guard threshold from 3 to 2 waiting robots. Measured against current: on-time 121.8 → 131.0 (+9.2, improved on 5/5 seeds), late 10.4 → 1.2, blocked s 2404 → 985, lowest on-time rate 0.84 → 0.98, unfinished stays 0.0. The KPI condition (>= 0.7) holds. Road violations rise from 25.8 to 34.0. Utility A / B / C moves from 38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8 to 45.4 / 37.2 / 19.0. Votes: A ○, B ×, C ×.
options.stakeholders: Gains: customers of all companies (far fewer late deliveries, and the worst-served company's on-time rate rises to 0.98) and company A (utility 38.4 → 45.4). Losses: company C (utility 28.8 → 19.0, a large drop), company B slightly (38.9 → 37.2), and possibly road safety and order, since road violations rise 25.8 → 34.0. Adopting it overrides the stated preference of two of the three companies.

options.summary: Raise the constitutional per-company on-time floor from 0.60 to 0.65. The current rules already meet the new condition (current lowest on-time rate is 0.84), so nothing changes in operation now. It only tightens the limit on future rule changes. It remains below the KPI condition of 0.7.
options.stakeholders: Gains: customers of the weakest company, who get a firmer legal guarantee against future rule changes that would leave them badly served. Losses: companies, slightly, because it narrows the set of rule changes they can adopt later. No immediate effect on any company's utility or on deliveries.

options.summary: Stay at v1: on-time 121.8, late 10.4, blocked s 2404, road violations 25.8, lowest on-time rate 0.84, utility A / B / C 38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8.
options.stakeholders: Gains: B and C keep their current utility, and their votes are respected. Losses: customers, who forgo about 9.2 more on-time deliveries and about 9.2 fewer late deliveries per run. Company A forgoes its utility gain.

recommendation.reason: It is the only option that moves the KPI. The main goal improves by +9.2 on 5/5 seeds, late deliveries drop from 10.4 to 1.2, and the KPI's fairness measure (lowest on-time rate) improves from 0.84 to 0.98, so no company's customers are worse served. However, it overrides B and C, C's utility falls sharply (28.8 → 19.0), and road violations rise (25.8 → 34.0). If you adopt it, consider recording why the override is justified and whether C should be compensated or the change reviewed after one period. R1 is harmless and can be decided separately, but it does not improve any measured outcome now.

unknowns: Why B and C voted against proposal 2, and what drives C's utility drop despite better on-time performance (e.g., cost, route share, or priority loss).
What the extra road violations under proposal 2 (34.0 vs 25.8) consist of, and whether they create safety risk or regulatory exposure.
How B and C will behave if overridden (strategic responses, reduced cooperation, or exit), which was not simulated.
How customers perceive the change, and whether they value the reduction in late deliveries as the KPI assumes.
Next period's demand level and pattern; results were measured on only 5 seeds of the current demand.
Whether the KPI floor of 0.7 will be revised after period 1, as the human indicated, and how R1 should relate to it.
Whether proposals 2 and R1 interact if both are adopted (not measured together).
